Version 2.0, October 2026

Executive summary

In July and August 2024, widespread protests resulted in the resignation of Awami League (AL) Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and the establishment of an interim government (IG) under the leadership of Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus, who was not affiliated to any political party.

On 12 February 2026, Bangladesh held a general election, which was generally considered to be democratic, fair and transparent. The Bangladesh National Party (BNP) received a majority of votes, and leader Tarique Rahman was sworn in as Prime Minister on 17 February 2026. The transition of power was reported to be peaceful. Jamaat-e-Islami (JeI) received the second largest number of votes in the election and are serving within the opposition. The AL were prohibited from running in the elections and remain a banned political party.

District committees have been set up by the Ministry of Home Affairs to review politically motivated cases lodged under the AL regime and, where cases are found to be politically motivated, they are recommended for withdrawal. The Bangladesh police indicated that, so far, around 500,000 individuals have had their cases withdrawn through this process. Members of the BNP and JeI who were previously charged under the AL government on politically motivated grounds have had their convictions overturned.

Leaders, members, and supporters of political groups in Bangladesh are unlikely to face a real risk of persecution or serious harm from the state, or from non-state/rogue state actors, on the grounds of their actual or perceived political opinion. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise.

In general, high profile and senior AL leaders, particularly those who held significant positions in the former government, are likely to face prosecution, rather than persecution, on the grounds of the actions committed under the former government, rather than due to their political opinion.

A person who has a well-founded fear of persecution or serious harm from a rogue state and/or non-state actor due to their actual or perceived political opinion is likely to obtain protection from the state and is likely to be able to internally relocate to escape that risk.

Where a claim from an actual or perceived BNP affiliate, supporter, member or leader, based on a fear of the state or non-state/rogue-state actors, is refused, it is likely to be certifiable as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

Other claims based on fear of the state or non-state/rogue-state actors are unlikely to be certifiable as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

All cases must be considered on their individual facts, with the onus on the person to demonstrate they face persecution or serious harm.

Assessment

Section updated: 30 September 2026

About the assessment

This section considers relevant evidence – including country information, refugee and human rights law and policy, and case law – to assess whether, in general:

a person faces a real risk of persecution/serious harm by state and/or non-state actors because of their political or imputed political opinion

the state (or quasi state bodies) can provide effective protection

internal relocation is possible to avoid persecution/serious harm

if refused, a claim is likely or not to be certified as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

For details on how CPIT makes its assessments, gathers and presents country information, its research methodology and disclaimers and explainers on coverage, source selection, maps, translations and the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in developing CPIT products, see About country policy and information notes.

1. Material facts, credibility and other checks

1.1.1 Decision makers must:

assess credibility (see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status

check if there has been a previous application for a UK visa or another form of leave. Asylum applications matched to visas should be investigated prior to the asylum interview (see the Asylum Instruction on Visa Matches, Asylum Claims from UK Visa Applicants).

consider making an international biometric data-sharing check, when one has not already been undertaken (see Biometric data-sharing process (Migration 5 biometric data-sharing process)).

consider language analysis testing, where available, in cases where there are doubts surrounding a person’s claimed place of origin (see the Asylum Instruction on Language Analysis).

2. Exclusion

2.1.1 Decision makers must consider whether there are serious reasons to apply one (or more) of the exclusion clauses. Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

2.1.2 Under the former Awami League (AL) government and during the student quota protests (July-August 2024), members of the security forces and AL members and affiliates have been accused of human rights abuses. The AL’s student wing, the Bangladesh Chhatra League (BCL) remains listed as a terrorist organisation under the current BNP government.

2.1.3 If the person is excluded from the Refugee Convention, they will also be excluded from a grant of humanitarian protection (which has a wider range of exclusions than refugee status).

2.1.4 For guidance on exclusion and restricted leave, see the Asylum Instruction on Exclusion under Articles 1F and 33(2) of the Refugee Convention, Humanitarian Protection and the instruction on Restricted Leave.

3. Convention reason(s)

3.1.1 Actual or imputed political opinion.

3.1.2 Establishing a convention reason is not sufficient to be recognised as a refugee. The question is whether the person has a well-founded fear of persecution on account of an actual or imputed Refugee Convention reason.

3.1.3 For further guidance on the 5 Refugee Convention grounds, see the Asylum Instruction, Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status.

4. Risk

4.1 Risk from the state

4.1.1 Leaders, members, and supporters of political groups in Bangladesh are unlikely to face a real risk of persecution or serious harm from the state on the grounds of their actual or perceived political opinion. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise.

4.1.2 In general, high profile and senior AL leaders, particularly those who held significant positions in the former government, are likely to face prosecution, rather than persecution, on the grounds of the actions committed under the former government, rather than due to their political opinion. The Bangladeshi government has a legitimate right to act against criminal acts and to use all lawful and proportionate means to do so. This includes seeking to prosecute those who have committed human rights abuses.

4.1.3 Those fleeing prosecution or punishment for a criminal offence are not normally refugees. However, prosecution may amount to persecution if it involves victimisation in its application by the authorities; for example, if it is the vehicle or excuse for the persecution of an individual or if only certain groups are prosecuted for a particular offence and the consequences of that discrimination are sufficiently severe. Punishment which is cruel, inhuman, or degrading (including punishment which is out of all proportion to the offence committed) may also amount to persecution. For information on the death penalty see the Country Policy and Information Note, Bangladesh: Actors of protection and the Asylum Instruction on Considering human rights claims.

4.1.4 To qualify for protection on the basis of a breach of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to a fair trial), the person must demonstrate a real risk of a flagrant violation of that right. The onus is on the person to do this. For further information see the Asylum Instruction on Considering human rights claims and the Country Policy and Information Note, Bangladesh: Actors of protection.

4.1.5 Bangladesh is a parliamentary democracy, with politics historically dominated by the AL and the Bangladesh National Party (BNP). The AL, led by Sheikh Hasina, were in power from 2009 to August 2024. From July 2024 to August 2024, an uprising developed from student-led protests against the government’s job quota system. On 5 August 2024, Sheikh Hasina resigned and fled to India. On 8 August 2024, an interim government (IG), led by Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus, who was not affiliated to any political party, was appointed (see Recent political events, Formation and tenure of the interim government (IG)).

4.1.6 On 17 July 2025, under the IG, Bangladesh acceded to the Optional Protocol to the UN Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment. The IG also created 6 commissions to instigate electoral, judicial, police, constitutional and public administration reform and to tackle corruption. The report of the 6 reform commissions was published in February 2025. Between March and October 2025, the constitutional reform commission held meetings with over 30 political parties and alliances to forge an agreement on political reforms, resulting in the July Charter which featured 84 reform proposals. It was endorsed by 24 political parties in October 2025, including the BNP and Jamaat-e-Islami (JeI). Although some signatory parties disagreed with certain provisions, it has been described as a ‘watershed’ moment in Bangladeshi political history (see Legislative, constitutional and policy reform).

4.1.7 The IG’s priority was to arrange elections, which were held on 12 February 2026 and were generally regarded as free and fair by international election observers. Alongside the election of a new government, the July Charter was taken to referendum where a ‘yes’ vote was secured. The BNP won the general election with a majority of votes, and party leader Tarique Rahman, who had returned from 17 years in the UK on 25 December 2025, was sworn in as the new Prime Minister. Jamaat-e-Islami (JeI) received the second highest number of votes and entered parliament as the official opposition. The transition of power was reported to be peaceful. Political groups continue to operate and there is strong and legitimate opposition in parliament and within communities (see 2026 elections, Election results and government formation, Treatment of political groups).

4.1.8 At local level, support is garnered through auxiliary groups affiliated with the main parties, the largest of which are student ‘wings’ (which can also include former students). These groups are active throughout Bangladesh’s educational institutes. While affiliated with national political parties, they are run at a local or regional level and their priorities, activities and degree of control by central party leadership varies. The AL-affiliated Bangladesh Chhatra League (BCL) has been banned for its role in violence under Hasina’s regime and during the 2024 protests (see Role, profile and membership of auxiliary organisations).

4.1.9 The activities of the AL were banned under the IG, and its registration was suspended by the Election Commission on 11 May 2025. The AL were unable to compete in the 2026 elections, and the new BNP government has upheld the ban. Although the party is not represented in Parliament and is unable to undertake formal political activities in the same manner as registered political parties, it continues to have members, supporters and a recognised political identity. The AL have conducted rallies across Bangladesh, although some were reported to involve criminal activity, and some participants have been arrested by the police (see Awami League (AL) and auxiliary organisations, Inter-party violence, Conduct of law enforcement personnel, Arrest and prosecution of Awami League members and affiliates under the BNP government).

4.1.10 Many AL leaders fled or went into hiding after former PM Hasina left Bangladesh and international travel bans have been placed on former AL ministers, high level officials, and their families. Tens of thousands of cases were lodged shortly after the IG was formed, mostly against high level members and leaders of the AL, including former ministers, members of parliament and lawmakers, for actions that took place under the former regime and during the protests. Several mass cases, involving unnamed defendants, were lodged during this period. Between February 2025 and March 2025, under a police operation to curb unrest and ensure public safety, over 12,000 people, mainly AL supporters, were arrested, some arbitrarily. This operation was suspended on 1 March 2025, and according to in-country sources interviewed by the Australian Government’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT), mass legal cases decreased in 2025 (see Awami League and affiliates, Arrest and prosecution of Awami League members and affiliates under the interim government, Accountability for corruption and abuses committed under the Awami League government).

4.1.11 Sources reported that there have been fewer arrests of AL members under the BNP government than under the IG. Sources told the Home Office FFM team in June 2026 that many AL members are being released on bail. The International Crime Tribunal (ICT), a domestic court which hears international crimes, and the regular justice system, continue to progress cases against AL members who committed human rights abuses under the AL government. In November 2025, the ICT reached its first verdict, sentencing Sheikh Hasina to death. On 15 September 2026, seven former ministers and senior officials of the AL received death sentences from the ICT (see Arrest and prosecution of Awami League members and affiliates under the BNP government, Accountability for corruption and abuses committed under the Awami League government).

4.1.12 The IG released thousands of prisoners detained during the July/August 2024 protests, alongside longer-term political prisoners who were detained under the AL regime. Sources told the Home Office FFM team in June 2026 that all of those detained for participating in the 2024 protests have since been released. On 8 April 2026, the July Mass Uprising (Protection and Liability Determination) Bill, providing legal protection for those who participated in the July 2024 uprising, was passed as law. Under this legislation, all civil and criminal complaints and legal proceedings relating to participation in the July 2024 uprising will be withdrawn and the filing of any new cases or complaints is legally prohibited. Cases relating to murder will be investigated (see Status of cases against participants in the July 2024 protests).

4.1.13 The Ministry of Home Affairs has set up District Committees (DC) to review alleged politically motivated cases lodged under the AL regime and, where cases are found to be politically motivated, recommend these for withdrawal. An affected person or their relatives can apply to the DC to have their case considered for withdrawal. On 30 April 2026, Bangladeshi media reported that 23,865 politically motivated cases lodged under the Hasina regime have been withdrawn. The Bangladesh police indicate that this is an ongoing process, and that, so far, around 500,000 individuals have had their cases withdrawn through this procedure. Members of the BNP and JeI who were previously charged under the AL government on politically motivated grounds have had their convictions overturned, including a senior leader of JeI, and BNP Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. Sources indicated to the Home Office FFM team that most of those detained on politically motivated charges made during the Hasina regime have been released, and most cases have been dismissed (see Status of politically-motivated criminal cases lodged under the Awami League government, BNP members and affiliates, Jamaat-e-Islami (JI or JeI) members and affiliates.

4.1.14 Arrest warrants in Bangladesh remain legally valid until they are executed or withdrawn during the judicial process, with no statutory time limits on their validity. According to the Bangladesh police, a person may go to court to request that a warrant is withdrawn. Sources indicate that, in practice, an arrest warrant for a politically motivated case under the AL regime may not be operationalised, or the person may be detained for a short period and then released while the case goes through the normal judicial process. Bail is possible, depending on the severity of the charges (see Status of politically-motivated criminal cases lodged under the AL government).

4.1.15 A small number of individuals have reportedly been arrested for criticising Prime Minister Tarique Rahman online. However, sources indicate that the surveillance of political opponents has decreased under the BNP government, and that generally, protests have been free from police interference. An MP from the National Citizen Party (NCP) told the Home Office FFM team in June 2026 that around 7 people had been arrested for publicly criticising the government in the previous 100 days, however it was not a widespread issue. Although journalists have been implicated in cases linked to the July 2024 uprising and, according to Reporters Without Borders, 5 were detained as of mid-2026, a local journalist told the Home Office FFM team that since the BNP government was elected, journalists could report freely (see Freedom of expression).

4.2 Risk from non-state actors

4.2.1 Leaders, members, and supporters of political groups are, in general, unlikely to face a real risk of persecution or serious harm from non-state actors and/or rogue state actors on the grounds of their actual or perceived political opinion. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise.

4.2.2 There were reports of intra- and inter-party violence during the pre-election period, as different parties and factions within parties sought influence ahead election including some violent demonstrations, mob attacks, clashes, vandalism, arson and extortion. However, most campaign events observed by the EU Election Observation Mission were generally peaceful, as was election day itself (see Political violence under the interim government, Security and anti-corruption efforts).

4.2.3 Sources reported to the Home Office FFM team in June 2026 that limited incidents have occurred in the period following the February 2026 election, and political violence has generally decreased under the BNP. Sources note that most incidents have involved ‘low-level’ violence such as shouting or throwing eggs (see Political violence in the post-election period).

4.2.4 Data from ACLED (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data) shows that mob violence, which can occur both within and outside of a protest environment, has decreased since the February 2026 election, with around 80 incidents in August 2026 compared to around 150 incidents in February 2026. Violent demonstrations also decreased in the same period, from around 25 in February 2026 to around 15 in August 2026. The same data indicated that most protest activity is peaceful, with around 250 peaceful protests in taking place in August 2026 (see Political violence under the interim government: Levels and nature of violence, Political violence in the post-election period: Levels and nature of violence).

4.2.6 Reporting from local media sources indicates that political parties suspended and expelled members who were involved in violence (see Political violence under the interim government: Inter-party violence, Political violence in the post-election period: Inter-party violence, BNP members and affiliates).

4.2.7 Sources told the Home Office FFM team that, although public sentiment towards the AL can be negative, members and supporters of the AL are generally safe in their communities. Some members of the AL have been absorbed into other political parties. In 2026, some AL lawyers reportedly won lawyers’ association elections with little resistance. Those who publicly express support for the AL, such as via social media or in organised demonstrations may be more likely to face harassment or hostility in their communities, and those who engaged in corruption or human rights abuses during the AL’s rule may face violence. However, a representative of the HRSS told the Home Office FFM team that although some AL members may fear mob violence, they are more likely to be handed over to the police by community members (see Awami League and affiliates).

4.2.8 For further guidance on assessing risk, see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status.

5. Protection

5.1.1 Where the person has a well-founded fear of persecution or serious harm from the state, they are unlikely to be able to obtain protection.

5.1.2 A person who has a well-founded fear of persecution or serious harm from a rogue state actor and/or a non-state actor on the grounds of their actual or perceived political opinion is likely to obtain protection from the state. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise.

5.1.3 In general, Bangladesh takes reasonable steps to prevent persecution by operating an effective legal system for the detection, prosecution and punishment of acts constituting persecution and a person is generally able to access this protection. Corruption, sympathy or weakness of some individuals in the system of justice does not mean that the state is unwilling to afford protection.

5.1.4 For information on protection generally, see the Country Policy and Information Note Bangladesh: Actors of protection.

5.1.5 The IG pursued a wide‑ranging reform agenda, centred on constitutional restructure, electoral and judicial reform, and anti‑corruption measures. The July Charter, a document outlining constitutional reforms which was negotiated by political parties during the IG’s rule and included as a referendum during the 2026 election, received a majority of ‘Yes’ votes (see Legislative, constitutional and policy reform, Election results).

5.1.6 The newly elected BNP government reviewed the ordinances made under the interim government related to reform and, although they have allowed some to lapse, they have converted most into law, including changes to the Code of Criminal Procedure to safeguard against arbitrary arrest. Some of the lapsed ordinances have subsequently been re-drafted and admitted into law such as the Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Redress Bill, and the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) Bill. These were passed in parliament on 7 September 2026, with some criticism from the opposition and civil society organisations, who considered them to provide weaker protections than the IG’s ordinances. Several sources told the UK Home Office Fact-Finding Mission (FFM) in June 2026 that progress on implementing the July Charter and broader reform recommendations has been limited, but many also acknowledged that it was still early in the new government’s tenure (see Reform of the security forces and judiciary and Reform agenda of the BNP government).

5.1.7 Sources indicate that concerns about politically motivated policing had reduced under the newly elected BNP government compared to the period of AL rule. Police representatives told the Home Office FFM team that all individuals, regardless of political affiliation, can access police protection and assistance, and that an individual can issue a complaint to police officials or the courts if they believe that police have not responded appropriately to their case. Non-governmental organisations also indicated that access to police protection is less politicised than during the AL government and that members and supporters of the political opposition are able to access police protection (see Conduct of law enforcement personnel).

5.1.8 Hundreds of senior officials and AL leaders under the former government have been arrested and remanded into custody in relation to deaths that occurred during the July/August 2024 protests and criminal acts that took place during the AL’s tenure in government. Other cases have been instigated against mayors, law enforcement personnel, and members of AL auxiliary organisations. Trials against those arrested are ongoing. The government has a legitimate right to act against criminal acts and to use all lawful and proportionate means to do so, including against those involved in criminal acts during the former regime and the protests (see Arrest and prosecution of Awami League members and affiliates under the interim government, Arrest and prosecution of Awami League members and affiliates under the BNP government, Accountability for corruption and abuses committed under the Awami League government).

5.1.9 For further guidance on assessing state protection, see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status.

6. Internal relocation

6.1.1 Where the person has a well-founded fear of persecution or serious harm from the state, they are unlikely to be able to internally relocate to escape that risk.

6.1.2 Where the person has a well-founded fear of persecution or serious harm from a non-state or rogue state actor, due to their actual or perceived political opinion, they are likely to be able to internally relocate to escape that risk. This is because in general, there are parts of country, such as (but not limited to) Dhaka, where it will be reasonable to expect them to relocate.

6.1.3 Bangladesh is a large country with a population of over 177 million people. Dhaka is the most populous city in Bangladesh, with a large urban population of 23.21 million people. For further information, and consideration of the reasonableness of internal relocation generally, see the Country Policy and Information Note Bangladesh: Internal relocation.

6.1.4 For consideration of internal relocation for women, see also the Country Policy and Information Note on Bangladesh: Women fearing GBV.

6.1.5 Members of the political opposition can, in general, internally relocate within Bangladesh. Leaders, members and supporters of the AL, who have had problems within their local communities, have relocated to other districts within Bangladesh following the July/August 2024 uprising, and some have returned to their home areas following the February 2026 general election (see Awami League and affiliates).

6.1.6 Low-level AL members, particularly those who have joined or reached understandings with other political parties, and those who are not publicly associated with corruption or human rights abuses committed under the previous AL government, do not generally face harassment in areas of relocation (see Awami League and affiliates).

6.1.7 Higher-profile AL members, particularly those accused of corruption or human rights abuses during the period of AL rule are likely to face adverse public attention. Sources reported that high-profile AL members had gone into hiding, but a representative of a Bangladeshi human rights organisation advised that such individuals would be more likely to be handed over to the police than subjected to violence in the community (see Awami League and affiliates, Risk, Protection).

6.1.8 For further guidance on internal relocation and factors to consider, see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status.

7. Certification

7.1.1 Where a claim from an actual or perceived BNP affiliate, supporter, member or leader, based on a fear of the state or non-state/rogue-state actors, is refused, it is likely to be certifiable as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

7.1.2 Other claims based on fear of the state or non-state/rogue-state actors are unlikely to be certifiable as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

7.1.3 Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

7.1.4 For further guidance on certification, see Certification of Protection and Human Rights claims under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 (clearly unfounded claims).

8. Political environment

8.1 Recent political events

8.1.1 The Awami League (AL), led by Sheikh Hasina, were in power from 2009 to August 2024.[footnote 1] From July 2024 to August 2024, an uprising developed from student-led protests against the government’s job quota system. Security forces cracked down on the protests, with around 1,400 deaths[footnote 2] and 20,000 injuries reported.[footnote 3] On 5 August 2024, Sheikh Hasina resigned and fled to India.[footnote 4]

8.1.2 On 8 August 2024, an interim government (IG), led by Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus, was appointed.[footnote 5] The IG banned the AL’s student wing (Bangladesh Chhatra League, BCL) in October 2024[footnote 6], and in May 2025 it banned all activities of the AL and affiliated organisations.[footnote 7]

8.1.3 On 12 February 2026, parliamentary elections were held.[footnote 8] The Bangladesh National Party (BNP) won a majority, and, on 17 February 2026, its leader Tarique Rahman was sworn in as Prime Minister.[footnote 9] [footnote 10] For an overview of the political situation up to November 2024, see:

8.2 Political system

8.2.1 For information on the structure of Bangladesh’s political system, see the archived Country Policy and Information Note Bangladesh: Political situation (December 2024).

9. Political parties

9.1 Role, profile and membership of auxiliary organisations

9.1.1 In its July 2025 Country Information Report on Bangladesh, based on various sources[footnote 11], the Australian government’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) noted:

‘The Awami League, the BNP and other political parties have large auxiliary organisations. They include ‘wings’ for students, volunteers, youth and professionals (e.g. doctors, lawyers and labourers). These organisations are sometimes known by other names, such as ‘fronts’ or ‘leagues’. The largest of these are the student wings, of which many former students are still members. Prior to the fall of the Hasina Government, the Awami League’s student wing, the Bangladesh Chhatra League (BCL), had millions of members. The BNP version, the Chhatra Dal, is also active …’[footnote 12]

9.1.2 The same report stated:

‘There are strong incentives to join an auxiliary organisation. For student organisations, members have access to better university accommodation, jobs upon graduation or business opportunities. Patronage is an important factor, attending protests or supporting a locally powerful person or politician offers protection. The poor are more vulnerable to these pressures (the rich can get opportunities without such networks), although membership of an auxiliary organisation does not guarantee employment.’[footnote 13]

9.1.3 Regarding a ban on student politics under the IG, on 9 August 2025 the Business Standard, a Dhaka based newspaper[footnote 14], reported that Dhaka University ‘… reaffirmed that the decision taken on 17 July last year to keep residential halls free from student politics remains in effect.’[footnote 15]

9.1.4 The Diplomat, an international current-affairs magazine covering Asia-Pacific[footnote 16], noted: ‘On September 19 [2024], the administration of the University of Dhaka decided to ban all kinds of student-teacher-staff politics on campus. Since the ouster of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s autocratic regime … 33 higher education institutes have banned student politics. Among them are 18 government universities, four government colleges, and 10 government medical colleges.’[footnote 17]

9.1.5 Despite the ban on student politics in Dhaka University, on 20 July 2026, LawNews24, a Dhaka based newspaper[footnote 18], reported:

‘Nearly two years after the July 2024 uprising called for an end to partisan politics in Dhaka University’s residential halls, mainstream student organizations have quietly re-established their presence, raising fresh questions over whether the movement’s pledge to depoliticize campus has faded.

‘Although no group has regained the overwhelming dominance once enjoyed by the now-banned Bangladesh Chhatra League (BCL), most major student organizations have formed hall committees or alternative structures to maintain their influence …

‘Bangladesh Islami Chhatra Shibir, now the strongest force in recent campus elections, maintains that it has no hall committees.

‘However, leaders of other student organizations allege that Shibir ‘hiddenly’ operates activities at the hall level.’[footnote 19]

9.1.6 On implementation of the ban in Dhaka University, the same article noted:

‘When asked, the current Vice-Chancellor [of Dhaka University] Dr A B M Obaidul Islam told Media … that he doesn’t have any such statement, document, or paper regarding student politics being banned.

‘“This matter of banning student politics — if it doesn’t come from the government, then even if I want to, or we want to, we’re not operating in a situation where we can just implement something like that on our own,” he added.

‘When asked if the current student administration has any plans to interfere with student politics in dormitories, he said, “No, we don’t have any such plan right now. If that kind of situation arises, we’ll see then.”’[footnote 20]

9.1.7 The DFAT 2025 report noted: ‘In January 2025, the Election System Reform Commission recommended to the Interim Government the prohibition of all political auxiliary organisations. This had not been implemented at the time of writing. Several universities have banned political activities on their grounds since August 2024.’[footnote 21] In the sources consulted, CPIT could not find any information or statement from the new BNP government on the implementation of this recommendation.

9.1.8 In June 2026, UK Home Office (UK HO) officials conducted a fact-finding mission (FFM) to Bangladesh to gather information from a range of sources on the political situation since July 2024. Regarding the role of auxiliary organisations and students in political parties, a political analyst at an international NGO told the UK HO FFM team that: ‘The important ones are the student, labour, youth, voluntary and women’s wings. They work as ‘brotherly or sisterly’ organisations or wings. They are important as they provide significant mobilisation power to each party.’[footnote 22]

9.1.9 When asked by the UK HO FFM team to explain the role of auxiliary organisations/student wings in political parties, and how they are aligned with the main parties, Abu Shadat Md Sayem, Monitoring Officer at Human Rights Support Society (HRSS), a Bangladesh-based human rights organisation[footnote 23], responded that: ‘Most of the parties have student auxiliaries, especially those aspiring to gain state power. Their first priority is to catch people at the university campus, as that’s where protests begin and spread. They always try to have their student wing in each university. AL had BCL [Bangladesh Chhatra League] etcetera.’[footnote 24]

9.1.10 When asked whether these auxiliary organisations are based in universities, the political analyst at the international NGO responded:

‘They have a presence in all educational institutions, and also in communities … The student wings have units in all administrative units of the country … They are students when they join these organisations, and there was a time when they would continue to be in the student organisation even after they finished. However … they no longer have members who are not studying in the universities, this changed around 2016/2017 onwards. AL and the BNP were the ones who decided to change that … this change is mostly visible in their campus units. For the units in the communities this is a work in progress …’[footnote 25]

9.1.11 When asked by the UK HO FFM team if there are any specific membership requirements for student wings, Abu Shadat Md Sayem responded that: ‘Generally, any student can become member of these student wings….

‘… there was no age limit, but they do say a student wing person should be a student … In reality, this is not the case. They have to attend lots of programmes, lots of rallies … they cannot keep up with their studies. In practice, most of the senior wing leaders are not students, or they are waiting to take their exams for 10 years for example.’[footnote 26]

14.4 Levels and nature of violence

14.4.1 ACLED collects information on political violence and protest events from multiple sources including media and local and international reporting.[footnote 226] In their recording of protests events, ACLED include ‘individuals and groups who peacefully demonstrate against a political entity, government institution, policy, group, tradition, business, or other private institution.’[footnote 227] A protest is defined by ACLED as: ‘…an in-person public demonstration of three or more participants in which the participants do not engage in violence, though violence may be used against them.’[footnote 228] The sub event type ‘violent demonstration’ is used when ‘demonstrators engage in violence and/or destructive activity’ and the sub-event type ‘mob violence’ is used ‘when rioters violently interact with other rioters, civilians or their property, or armed groups outside of demonstration contexts. A mob is considered a crowd of people that is disorderly and has the intention to cause harm or disruption through violence or property destruction. Note that this type of violence can also include spontaneous vigilante mobs clashing with other armed groups or attacking civilians.’[footnote 229] For more information on ACLED terminology, see its Methodology.

‘… Police have pursued criminal charges against journalists for what was seen as backing the Hasina government in their reporting during the Monsoon Revolution [the July-August 2024 uprising] …

16.7 Status of politically-motivated criminal cases lodged under the Awami League government

16.7.1 HRW noted in January 2025 ‘…the IG It has said it will drop police investigations and charges against peaceful critics of Sheikh Hasina, her relatives and associates, and her administration …’[footnote 374]

16.7.2 The DFAT 2025 report noted: ‘… In April 2025, the Interim Government indicated it would publish a list of politically motivated cases (filed between 6 January 2009 and 5 August 2024, numbering in the thousands) it would recommend be withdrawn.’[footnote 375]

16.7.3 Regarding the publishing and withdrawal of politically motivated cases under the previous Awami League government, on 30 April 2026, Bangladesh Sangbad Sangstha (BSS News), a Bangladesh news agency[footnote 376], noted:

‘A total of 23,865 politically motivated harassment cases have so far been withdrawn, and the process to withdraw the remaining cases is currently underway, Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Md Asaduzzaman told the Jatiya Sangsad [Bangladesh Parliament] today …

‘… he said the government does not have precise statistics on the number of harassment cases filed against leaders and activists of BNP and Jamaat-e-Islami across the country.

‘The minister explained that political identity is not mentioned in the First Information Report (FIR) at the time of filing a case, making it difficult to determine such figures accurately.

‘However, citing information received from BNP’s central office, he said that from 2007 to 11 January, 2025, a total of 142,983 false and harassment cases were filed against BNP leaders and activists.

‘“No official data is available regarding such cases filed against Jamaat-e-Islami leaders and activists during the same period,” he added.

‘The minister further said that after assuming office, the current [BNP] government formed a four-member district-level committee on 5 March, 2026, headed by the district magistrate, to review and recommending for withdrawal of politically motivated cases.

‘The committee reviews applications for withdrawal along with FIRs, certified copies of charge sheets (where applicable), and opinions from Public Prosecutors (PPs).

‘“If a case is found to have been filed for political harassment, is not necessary in the public interest, and its continuation may harm the state, it recommends the case for withdrawal,” he added.

‘To facilitate the process, a six-member central committee, headed by the Law Minister, was formed on 8 March, 2026, to examine district-level recommendations and take necessary actions regarding case withdrawals.’[footnote 377]

16.7.4 The human rights activist and political analyst associated with ASK advised the UK HO FFM team that ‘In the past, there were hundreds and thousands of cases under the AL against Jamaat and BNP, the political opponents. After the IG came to power, they dismissed most of the cases, though a few cases are maybe still pending.’[footnote 378]

16.7.5 Representatives from the Bangladesh Police told the UK HO FFM team that: ‘… There were a lot of political cases which didn’t seem to be accurate. We agreed with our Ministry of Home Affairs to form a District Committee, which would allow someone who thought they had a false case to appeal to the committee who would look into matters. If it was found to be unjust then the Committee could recommend withdrawal of the case.’[footnote 379]

16.7.6 The UK HO FFM team asked whether they were referring to politically motivated cases lodged under the Hasina regime, to which representatives from the Bangladesh Police responded: ‘Yes, and soon after the AL’s departure there were some cases registered during the student uprising … Someone can claim a case is false and malicious, he can appeal to a District Committee, and they will decide to recommend it to MoHA [Ministry of Home Affairs] to withdraw.’[footnote 380]

16.7.7 When asked by the UK HO FFM team to explain the process of getting a politically motivated case withdrawn, the representatives from the Bangladesh Police responded that: ‘You go to the district committee and appeal to district level. You put in a plea for withdrawal, and they will examine the allegations.’[footnote 381]

16.7.8 When asked by the UK HO FFM team who would raise the issue of a politically motivated case and whether the government identifies these cases, the representatives from the Bangladesh Police responded that:

‘An accused person or their relatives may apply to have their warrant withdrawn.

‘We have a well-structured procedure. The accused person or relative may apply to the district. We have 64 districts, 64 committees. At district level, the application is reviewed within 15 working days through the public prosecutor. If it is identified as politically-motivated, or harassment-related, we withdraw the case, then a recommendation is forwarded to the Ministry of Home Affairs. Then if it goes back to the district magistrate, to the court, the court issues an order, and the process is complete and comes to an end.’[footnote 382]

16.7.9 Regarding the number of withdrawn politically motivated cases, the representatives from the Bangladesh Police told the UK HO FFM team that ‘… 21,585 cases have already been withdrawn …’ and ‘… More cases have been examined, and more cases will be withdrawn I believe.’[footnote 383]

16.7.10 In addition, representatives from the Bangladesh Police continued: ‘There have been recommendations by the government, from district level or committee which we have in metropolitan areas. We believe it has given relief to 500,000 individuals. It’s a continuous process and recommendations are still coming to districts, magistrates or the committee, to withdraw cases.’[footnote 384]

16.7.11 When asked by the UK HO FFM on the status of those held on politically motivated charges under the Hasina regime, the political analyst at an International NGO responded that ‘Most of those arrested have been released after August 2024, by early 2025, under the IG.’[footnote 385]

16.7.12 Regarding those who had been arrested on politically motivated charges under the Hasina government, Saiful Islam of the HRSS clarified that ‘Most of the political[ly motivated] cases filed during the Hasina regime were dismissed. Some of the major cases are pending but the accused got bailed.

‘Major accused and arrested persons were leaders and supporters of both BNP and BJI [Jamaat] and their student wings.’[footnote 386]

16.7.13 Abu Shadat Md Sayem of the HRSS told the UK HO FFM team that ‘The people who were arrested under the Hasina regime, most are free. Two who were on death row are now free.’[footnote 387]

16.7.14 When asked by the UK HO FFM team if those held on politically motivated charges remained in custody, Mir Ahmad Bin Quasem, JeI MP, responded:

‘Most people held on politically motivated charges under Sheikh Hasina’s government, including those with a political background, have been released. However, some people accused of crimes during the 1971 Liberation War are still in prison. The fate of these cases hasn’t changed much. Also, those held for the border guard mutiny during the AL, 175 have been executed so far, and those who were not executed but serving a life sentence are still inside.’[footnote 388]

16.7.15 When asked by the UK HO FFM team if a politically motivated arrest warrant issued under the Hasina government would still be enforced, the advisor at an NGO responded:

‘There were a number of false cases dismissed during the IG period. They did a whole exercise where a significant number of cases against these individuals were dismissed. There was obviously a procedure to go through to dismiss cases depending on the stage of the case and the judge etcetera.

‘There were a number of individuals who have cases against them but they are inactive and they are being not followed through. This is the same as the policy under the IG with cases that were politically motivated and enacted during the AL government. These are not prosecuted anymore. Cases are seen through. The person accused will appear at hearings and the case will run through and end, or the charges are dismissed.

‘Although it does depend of [sic] the charges/type of case, police cases can’t be dismissed. For example, if a criminal case was filed against me for murder, the police can’t show up to the judge and ask for the case to be dropped. There is a procedure to follow on certain cases, but the expectation [for politically motivated cases] is that it won’t amount to anything and the judge will close the case.’[footnote 389]

16.7.16 The UK HO FFM team asked if an arrest warrant issued under the Hasina government against a political opponent would still be valid. The human rights activist and political analyst associated with ASK responded that: ‘No, they won’t be operationalised at this moment, because the cases are lifted so the warrant won’t work at this moment. We are seeing most of the BNP activists who were hiding to dodge the process, they are now mostly free so they are walking around the streets, participating in the political activities of the BNP and JeI. Their concern has gone away …’[footnote 390]

16.7.17 When asked by the UK HO FFM team if an arrest warrant issued against a political opponent during the Hasina regime would still legally stand, and the process of executing a warrant, Mir Ahmad Bin Quasem, JeI MP, responded: ‘Legally, there is no time limit on the validity of a warrant, unless there is a revision by law or it is taken back by the relevant police department. If there [is] no action taken to withdraw the warrant, then it remains valid indefinitely. That is the legal position.

‘But, in practice, the police are understaffed, overburdened and underfunded. Even a valid warrant may never really be enforced.’[footnote 391]

16.7.18 Mir Ahmad Bin Quasem, JeI MP, told the UK HO FFM team that:

‘I know of 2 Jamaat leaders who, due to a fear of prosecution, fled during the AL rule and when they returned, they were detained at the airport. They were taken to court and released on bail. One warrant was in place for 7 years and now that there is a digital system, a warrant will remain there forever and you can get caught no matter how many years later. Those with existing warrants may get arrested on return, they may get bail or may be detained for a few days, or after a long time, it depends on the degree of severity of the charges.’[footnote 392]

16.7.19 The UK HO FFM team asked if the warrant would still go through the court process. Mir Ahmad Bin Quasem confirmed that ‘Yes, it has to go through the legal process and then they get bail. One of the senior religious leaders accused by the AL had to go through the legal process to get out. He spent time in jail but then got out and the case was closed.’[footnote 393]

16.7.20 The UK HO FFM team asked what was the legal status of arrest warrants that had not been executed. Representatives from the Bangladesh Police responded:

‘The arrest warrant is a part of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It remains valid until it is put into action. There are some exceptions; if the person goes to court and receives bail, the warrant is withdrawn because they have already appeared before court, or if someone is dead, or if any cases are withdrawn, that is the usual disposal. Some people have had cases withdrawn even if they haven’t appealed, but if the person did not go to the court then the arrest warrant is not withdrawn, so they have to proceed to the court to ask for it to be withdrawn. If a person goes to court with a recommendation for the case to be withdrawn they can keep a copy of that with them, so they have it in case law enforcement go to their house, so it can be mitigated but they have to go the court to get it withdrawn. We do not have the system in place to share this between police stations. This is the process. But even if someone is apprehended and taken to the court, he can show the papers to the court that the case has been withdrawn and they will be released.’[footnote 394]

17. Freedom of expression

17.1 Assembly and association

17.1.1 In relation to the IG’s tenure, the BTI 2026 report noted:

‘… under the IG, no systematic interference with the rights of assembly and association was observed. Instead, the restoration of assembly rights prompted many groups to protest and voice long-suppressed demands, often by blocking roads and busy intersections in the capital. Students and professionals, along with religious and social groups who felt aggrieved or discriminated against under AL rule, began demonstrating for pay raises, benefits and changes to socio-religious policy.’[footnote 403]

17.1.2 When asked by the UK HO FFM if people were able to protest and assemble, Navid Nowroz Shah MP responded that ‘Yes, people can protest now, the situation is okay, but … there have been a few incidents … the BNP are not putting any pressure on police, but if we as a party organise a protest or assemble, some people have been attacked by the BNP. But the situation is not that bad …’[footnote 404]

17.1.3 When asked by the UK HO FFM team whether there was a difference in police response depending on the topic of protests (for example, land rights versus political), Navid Nowroz Shah responded: ‘No, I don’t think so … But if you … criticise the prime minister then the situation gets worse … A few people have spoken out against [PM] Tarique Rahman, they have been arrested, but this is not the general scenario.’[footnote 405]

17.1.4 Regarding freedom of expression in the post-election period, the political analyst at an International NGO told the UK HO FFM team that ‘In general, JeI and NCP … they are not protesting that much. However, we have seen them protest when they want, and some ‘soft’ protests. So far there is no evidence that they have been oppressed.’[footnote 406]

17.1.5 Zeeba Khan, BNP MP told the UK HO FFM team that: ‘I think all political parties can now operate freely. None of us could operate freely before … So, our whole politics changed.’[footnote 407]

17.2 Media and social media

17.2.1 Regarding charges against journalists under the interim government, on 6 May 2025, the Daily Star reported: ‘… This newspaper has found at least 266 journalists have been implicated in various cases related to the events of the July [2024] uprising.’[footnote 408]

17.2.2 On 15 June 2025, the Dhaka Tribune reported:

‘Addressing the issue of cases against journalists, Adviser Asif Nazrul [law adviser to the interim government] said: “A total of 266 journalists have been sued, but only 15 have been arrested. The cases were filed for insider crimes or for amendments.”

‘He added: “These were not initiated by the government—they were filed by ordinary citizens. However, we have made it clear that no arrests should be made unless there is substantial evidence.” …

‘When asked about the bail of two journalists from Ekattor TV, Asif Nazrul said: “I understand there are objections regarding the arrests. As far as I know, the charges against them were not filed for journalism.”

‘He added: “Whether they deserve bail is a valid question, but the case itself was filed by members of the public, and we have no role in that.”’[footnote 409]

17.2.3 In relation to murder charges against journalists relating to the July 2024 uprising, on 5 May 2026, the Economic Express, a Bangladeshi newspaper[footnote 410], reported: ‘Zahed Ur Rahman, prime minister’s adviser on information and broadcasting, has said that filing specific murder cases against journalists arrested over the July [2024] Uprising was a wrong move. 17.2.4 Regarding charges against journalists who are perceived to be affiliated with the Awami League, on 15 May 2026, the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) noted:

‘On May 14 [2026], the ICT in the capital Dhaka showed [Farzana] Rupa, a former chief reporter and presenter at privately owned Ekattor TV, and [Mozammel] Babu, the channel’s founder and former editor-in-chief, arrested in a case linked to the May 2013 crackdown on a rally by Islamist group Hefajat-e-Islam at Shapla Chattar. ‘Rupa and Babu have been held in pre-trial detention since August and September 2024, respectively, in connection with separate murder cases linked to deaths during the July 2024 mass uprising …’[footnote 412]

17.2.5 As of 21 September 2026, Reporters without Borders, an international non-profit organisation focussed on ‘… the defence and promotion of freedom of information …’[footnote 413], recorded that there are 5 journalists currently detained in Bangladesh.[footnote 414] Of these 5 journalists, 3 have been detained since the 17 September 2024 and 2 have been detained since 21 August 2024.[footnote 415] Journalists are only listed if ‘… RSF has established that their death or imprisonment was linked to their journalistic activity …’.[footnote 416]

17.2.6 Regarding the situation for journalists who had been arrested under the interim government, the activist and analyst associated with ASK told the UK HO FFM team in June 2026 that: ‘They got bail, but their cases are not withdrawn so they are awaiting trial.’[footnote 417]

17.2.7 Regarding journalists who were arrested under the interim government, Ayesha Kabir told the UK HO FFM team that: ‘… a lot of them are still in jail. Some have been released and some cases are still going on …

‘Recently, many of them have been released …’[footnote 418]

17.2.8 Regarding freedom of expression under the newly elected government, on 22 April 2026 Prothom Alo reported: ‘… [A] demonstration was organised demanding the release of AM Hasan Nasim, who was arrested by police on 18 April [2026] on allegations of spreading misleading information on Facebook about the Chief Whip of Parliament, Nurul Islam.

‘Protesters, however, claimed that his arrest was triggered merely by sharing a cartoon on Facebook. He was granted bail later the same afternoon.’ [footnote 419]

17.2.9 The same source reported: ‘A series of recent arrests linked to social media posts has once again raised concerns over freedom of expression. In the past month alone, at least four individuals were arrested under Section 54, the Anti-Terrorism Act, and the Cyber Security Act, while another person was taken into police custody …’[footnote 420]

17.2.10 On 23 April 2026, a Human Rights Watch news release stated: ‘On April 2 [2026], members of the ruling party’s youth wing, Jubo Dal, abducted Shaon Mahmud and handed him over to the police in Sreenagar, near Dhaka, for allegedly “insulting” the prime minister on Facebook. 17.2.11 Navid Nowraz Shah, NCP MP, told the UK HO FFM team that ‘… There have been some incidents in the past 100 days, 6 or 7 people have been arrested for criticising the government which has been a negative, but still the situation is better than before. 17.2.12 When asked by the UK HO FFM team if the newly elected government are interested in social media posts, the political analyst at an international NGO responded: ‘… the BNP does not seem to have such a strict control [over social media posts]. Annex A: Responses to questions sent to British High Commission, Dhaka

Date of issue: 29 September 2026

How has the political environment changed since August 2024?

Since August 2024, Bangladesh has undergone a significant political transition. Following the student-led uprising and the departure of the previous government, an interim government led by Professor Muhammad Yunus was formed on 8 August 2024. The interim administration subsequently established a number of reform commissions covering the constitution, electoral system, judiciary, public administration, policing and anti-corruption institutions.

The reform process was accompanied by consultations with political parties and other stakeholders, leading to a broader consensus-building process and the July National Charter. Elections were subsequently held in February 2026, resulting in the formation of a Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP)-led government. The EU Election Observation Mission (EU EOM) described the elections as credible and genuinely competitive, noting a revitalised civic space and broad respect for fundamental freedoms during the campaign period.

How have the changes affected political groups?

The political transition has reshaped Bangladesh’s political landscape. The period has seen greater political participation by a range of political actors, including established opposition parties, newly formed political parties and student-led political movements. It has also created opportunities for political parties and civil society organisations to contribute to discussions on governance and institutional reform.

The impact has varied across different political groups. Parties that had previously been in opposition have assumed a more prominent role in political life and electoral politics. At the same time, the Awami League has faced significant legal and operational restrictions.

Has the newly elected BNP government implemented any recommendations from commissions formed under the interim government? If so, what?

The commissions established by the interim government informed a number of ordinances (laws or regulations) and reform proposals across areas including constitutional, electoral, judicial, public administration, police and anti-corruption reform. These recommendations were subsequently considered through the National Consensus Commission process and reflected in the July National Charter.

Following the election, Parliament reviewed 133 ordinances promulgated during the interim period. A special parliamentary committee recommended that 98 ordinances be approved, 15 be amended before enactment, and 20 not be approved in their existing form. Under Bangladesh’s constitutional framework, ordinances not approved by Parliament lapse, although revised legislation may subsequently be introduced through the normal legislative process.

What is the current status of the Awami League (legally, in theory and in practice)?

The Awami League’s political activities were prohibited under measures introduced during the interim administration in 2025, and the party’s registration was cancelled, preventing its participation in the February 2026 parliamentary elections. Parliament subsequently enacted legislation maintaining those restrictions.

The party is not represented in Parliament and is unable to undertake formal political activities in the same manner as registered political parties. However, the Awami League continues to have members, supporters and a recognised political identity.

While the party and its supporters continue to engage in political advocacy and commentary, including through statements from party leaders, online platforms and activities conducted from outside Bangladesh, these activities take place within the context of the legal and operational restrictions currently in force. Public organisational activity within Bangladesh remains limited by those restrictions.

What is the role of the auxiliary organisations (particularly student wings) in political parties?

Auxiliary organisations, including student, youth, labour and professional wings, have long been a feature of Bangladesh’s political landscape. They are typically affiliated with larger political parties and play an important role in political mobilisation, leadership development, advocacy and outreach. Student organisations in particular have often served as an entry point into politics, with many national political leaders beginning their political careers through student activism.

Following the events of 2024, student groups have received increased public attention given the prominent role played by students in the protests that preceded the political transition. The period since then has also seen the emergence of new student-led political initiatives and parties.

Any legal / legislative restrictions on operation for political parties?

Political parties are generally able to organise and participate in political activity within Bangladesh’s legal framework. Political parties remain subject to applicable laws governing registration, elections, public order and political activity.

The restrictions on Awami League are covered in an earlier question.

Are members / supporters of political organisations able to express their views / protest?

The Constitution of Bangladesh provides for freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly. Members and supporters of political parties, civil society organisations and other groups continue to express their views through public statements, meetings, social media, rallies and protests.

Since the political transition of 2024, a broad range of political actors, including established parties, newly formed political groups, student-led movements, religious organisations, civil society groups and issue-based movements have participated in public debate and political activity.

The position of the Awami League is distinct, given the legal restrictions currently in force on the party’s activities. While Awami League leaders, members and supporters continue to express political views, the party is not able to organise and participate in political activities in the same manner as other political parties.

More broadly, domestic and international human rights organisations have reported human rights concerns in relation to detention, politically motivated arrests and prosecutions involving political actors. While many reported cases have involved individuals associated with the former Awami League administration, concerns have also been raised regarding the treatment of political opponents, activists and public figures more generally.

Political demonstrations and rallies continue to take place in Bangladesh. However, there are periodic reports of tensions and clashes between supporters of different political groups.

What is the police response to protest? Are there differences in response under the Awami League, the Interim Government and the current government?

The July-August 2024 protests were marked by significant unrest and the use of force by security forces, which subsequently became the subject of domestic and international scrutiny and prompted wide-ranging discussions on police reform and accountability.

Following the July 2024 Uprising and political transition, police reform was identified as a priority area by the interim government and examined through the Police Reform Commission. The EU Election Observation Mission found that the 2026 elections took place in a substantially different environment, describing the elections as credible and noting that polling day was peaceful. Nonetheless, it recorded sporadic localised political violence and highlighted concerns regarding protection from harassment and intimidation in some instances.

What were the levels of pre-election / election period intra- and inter-party violence? How does this compare to levels under the Awami League?

The EU Election Observation Mission (EU EOM) assessed the 2026 parliamentary elections as credible and genuinely competitive, noting that fundamental freedoms were broadly respected and that polling day was peaceful. The EU EOM nevertheless recorded sporadic localised incidents of political violence and intimidation during the campaign period.

Observers generally noted a more open and competitive political environment than during recent electoral cycles. The EU EOM described the polls as the first genuinely competitive parliamentary elections since 2008 and highlighted a revitalised civic space during the campaign period.

Any inter- / intra-party violence post-election? What was the police response?

There have continued to be reports of localised incidents of both inter-party and intra-party violence following the election, particularly in relation to local political rivalries, competition for influence and disputes within party structures. However, these incidents have generally been localised rather than indicative of widespread national unrest.

The police have continued to respond through their normal law enforcement responsibilities, including maintaining public order, providing security at political events, investigating allegations of violence and making arrests where offences are alleged to have occurred. However, a number of observers have noted continuing challenges in relation to law and order and public confidence in law enforcement following the events of 2024.

Any violence by the state? If so, by whom and, if security forces, which security forces?

Since the political transition of August 2024, allegations of violence or misconduct by state actors have continued to be reported, although the scale and nature of such allegations differ from those associated with the July-August 2024 protests. Reporting by human rights organisations and other observers has focused primarily on allegations relating to arrests, detention practices, treatment of individuals in custody, and the conduct of security forces in maintaining public order.

Where allegations have involved security forces, they have most commonly concerned the Bangladesh Police, including metropolitan and district police units responsible for law enforcement and public order functions. Human rights organisations have also continued to monitor the conduct of other security and intelligence agencies.

Questions relating to accountability, oversight of security institutions, police reform and public confidence in law enforcement remain part of the broader governance and reform agenda that emerged following the political transition.

Can journalists operate freely? Are there legal or practical barriers?

Journalists in Bangladesh continue to report on a wide range of political, social and economic issues. The 2026 EU Election Observation Mission noted a revitalised civic space and found that fundamental freedoms were broadly respected during the election period.

At the same time, journalists continue to face legal and practical challenges, including concerns relating to digital security legislation, online harassment, disinformation, self-censorship and pressures associated with reporting on politically sensitive issues. The EU EOM also highlighted incidents of digital violence and harassment and noted concerns regarding the adequacy of protection for media actors in some cases.

Domestic and international organisations have also raised concerns regarding criminal proceedings involving some journalists and the potential impact of such cases on media freedom and freedom of expression.

Women journalists may face additional challenges, including gender-based harassment and abuse, particularly in online spaces.

Can NGOs / CSOs operate freely? Are there legal or practical barriers?

Civil society organisations, NGOs, think tanks, professional associations and advocacy groups continue to operate in Bangladesh and play an active role in public life, development activities and policy discussions. Since the political transition of August 2024, civil society actors have participated in consultations on governance and institutional reform, and many observers have noted a more open civic environment than in previous years.

At the same time, NGOs and CSOs continue to operate within a regulatory framework that includes requirements relating to registration, funding, reporting and compliance. Organisations working on governance, human rights and politically sensitive issues may encounter administrative, legal or operational challenges.

Have people who took part in the July protests been arrested, detained, prosecuted or released?

During and immediately following the July-August 2024 protests, large numbers of individuals were arrested or detained. Following the political transition, the UN and other observers reported that thousands of detainees were released and that a number of cases were subsequently reviewed. At the same time, investigations and legal proceedings relating to allegations of violence and other offences connected to the events of 2024 have continued in some instances.

Is there an update on those held on allegedly politically motivated charges under Hasina? Do people remain in custody? What is the profile of such people?

Following the political transition in August 2024, the authorities reviewed a number of cases that had been criticised by political parties, civil society organisations and human rights groups as politically motivated. A significant number of opposition politicians, activists and other individuals who had been detained under the previous administration were subsequently released, granted bail, or had cases reviewed, withdrawn or dismissed.

However, outcomes have varied depending on the individual case, and some proceedings continue before the courts. Those affected have included politicians and activists from opposition parties, as well as journalists, civil society actors and other public figures.

Domestic and international organisations have continued to emphasise the importance of ensuring that all cases are assessed on the basis of evidence and in accordance with due process, fair trial guarantees and judicial independence.
